title: The "font" Top-Level Media Type
summary: Registers the top-level media type font, under which font formats can be registered, along with intended subtypes that were previously registered under application.

plainLanguage.summary: Gives fonts their own labeled drawer instead of the miscellaneous one.

questions: what is the font top-level media type
what is the difference between font/ttf and font/otf
are font files a security risk
subtitle: Gives fonts their own top-level media type, so web servers can label font files as font/woff, font/ttf and friends.

tldr.problem: Web fonts had no intuitive media type. Fonts were registered under application, but most sites used unregistered guesses or generic types such as application/octet-stream.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8081 registers font as a new top-level media type and registers six subtypes under it: sfnt, ttf, otf, collection, woff and woff2.
tldr.outcome: The older application/font-sfnt and application/font-woff registrations are deprecated in favor of font/sfnt and font/woff. Fonts can carry hidden data and executable hints, so the RFC warns that they need careful handling.

today: RFC 8081 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It deprecates the older application/font-sfnt and application/font-woff registrations in favor of font/sfnt and font/woff.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Fonts supply the visual shapes (glyphs) that text systems draw. Early fonts were often bitmaps tuned for a given size on low-resolution displays. More recently, scalable vector outline fonts have come into widespread use, where the system renders the outline at the desired position and size.

Internet media types label content carried over Internet protocols. RFC 8081 defines a new top-level type, font, following Section 4.2.7 of RFC 6838. The top-level type says the content is font data, and different font formats are registered as subtypes beneath it.
sections.plainLanguage: A font is a set of instructions for drawing letters. This RFC makes a new label that says 'this file is a font'.

sections.title: Why a Font Type Was Needed
sections.content:
Before this RFC there was no registration of formats for fonts, and some formats were registered under the application top-level type, for example application/font-woff. The text cites HTTP Archive data showing web font use rising from 1% of sites at the end of 2010 to 50% at the beginning of 2015.

The analysis the RFC cites found that registered font types saw very limited use. Many sites instead used intuitive but nonexistent types such as font/woff, font/ttf and font/truetype. Most sites fell back on generic types such as application/octet-stream, text/plain and text/html, or on unregisterable types such as application/x-font-ttf.

The W3C WebFonts working group gave three reasons against the application tree. It is treated with great caution for viruses and other active code. A top-level type allows a common set of optional parameters. Fonts also have a unique set of licensing and usage restrictions that justify their own category. The group pointed to the image tree, where correct media type usage reaches over 97%, as the model.
sections.plainLanguage: Everybody was already making up their own labels for fonts, and many just wrote 'mystery file'. A proper label that is easy to guess makes it simpler for everyone to agree.

sections.title: What the font Type Means
sections.content:
The font type tells a receiver that the content needs a graphic subsystem, such as a font rendering engine and sometimes a text layout and shaping engine. That may in turn require a certain level of CPU performance and memory. The top-level type says nothing about the data format; the subtype names the specific font format.

A receiver that sees an unrecognized font subtype should treat it as application/octet-stream. It may instead pass it to a common font-handling system if one is available.

New formats are registered with the online form, consulting RFC 6838. The font specification should preferably be freely available, and a format that can hold multiple fonts should also define a fragment identifier syntax. If a receiver does not recognize a sub-value in a comma-separated parameter list, it should ignore it and continue with the others.
sections.plainLanguage: The big label says 'this is a font'. A smaller label says which kind. If a computer does not know the kind, it treats the file as a plain mystery file.

sections.title: The Six Registered Subtypes
sections.content:
The RFC registers six subtypes and says they also serve as examples for future registrations. Each lists an @font-face format identifier for the CSS3 Fonts specification, which is normative; the identifiers in the RFC are informative.

  • font/sfnt is an abstract type from which font/ttf and font/otf are conceptually derived. It is expected to be rare in practice.
  • font/ttf is for TrueType fonts, with @font-face format truetype.
  • font/otf is for OpenType Layout fonts, with format opentype.
  • font/collection holds several fonts in one file, with extension .ttc.
  • font/woff is WOFF 1.0 and font/woff2 is WOFF 2.0. The RFC says the two formats have different media types and may be used in parallel.

The sfnt, ttf and otf registrations point to ISO/IEC 14496-22 "Open Font Format" as the published specification, with ISO/IEC holding change control. The WOFF types are controlled by the W3C. All six are marked for COMMON intended usage with no restrictions on usage.
sections.plainLanguage: There are six drawers inside the font cabinet, one for each common kind of font file. Some are for single fonts and one is for a bundle of fonts in one file.

sections.title: Optional Parameters and File Markers
sections.content:
The sfnt registration defines two optional parameters. outlines is a comma-separated subset of TTF, CFF and SVG and says what kind of glyph outlines the font holds. layout is a comma-separated subset of OTL, AAT and SIL, for OpenType layout, Apple Advanced Typography and Graphite SIL. Order in either list is not significant.

The parameters exist because one font file can hold the same glyphs in several representations. A rendering engine that cannot process any of them would waste a download, so the parameters let applications decide sooner. The ttf subtype defines only layout, while otf and collection define only outlines. WOFF and WOFF2 define none.

The registrations also list magic numbers. TrueType outlines use 0x00010000 as the sfnt version number, and OpenType fonts with CFF outlines use the tag OTTO. A WOFF file's signature field must contain 0x774F4646 ('wOFF'), and a WOFF2 file's must contain 0x774F4632 ('wOF2').
sections.plainLanguage: Extra notes can say what is inside the font, a bit like a sticker on a lunchbox saying which snacks are inside. Special first bytes in the file also act like a secret handshake that says what kind of font it is.

sections.title: Fragment Identifiers for Font Collections
sections.content:
A font collection file holds several fonts. A fragment identifier picks one by its PostScript name (name ID 6). That name is a string of at most 63 printable ASCII characters, codes 33 to 126, except ten forbidden characters: [ ] ( ) { } < > / %.

Six more characters that could appear in a PostScript name are not allowed in URI fragments by RFC 3986, so they must be escaped: the double quote, the number sign, the backslash, the caret, the grave accent and the vertical bar. For example, #Foo-Bold refers to the font named Foo-Bold, and #Caret%5Estick refers to the font named Caret^stick.

If the name does not match, or no fragment is given, the first font in the collection is used. The RFC warns that font order can change when the collection is revised, so relying on the first font is unwise.
sections.plainLanguage: If a book holds many fonts, you can ask for one by its name. If you ask for a name that is not there, you get the first one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Fonts are interpreted data structures made of many tables: glyph outlines, hinting instructions, metrics, layout rules and more. Hints for TrueType glyphs can be executable code that could be maliciously built, for example to hang the interpreter. Even though hints run inside the font rendering engine with no access outside it, a complex malicious font could use excessive memory or CPU, and the RFC says most interpreters cannot be completely protected without undue performance penalties.

The SFNT format is extremely flexible and extensible, which also makes it easy to hide arbitrary data inside a font file. The RFC sees a significant risk that this could be used to hide malicious binary content disguised as a font data component.

Font formats offer data integrity mechanisms such as checksums and digital signatures, but no privacy or confidentiality protection. If needed, that protection should be provided externally.
sections.plainLanguage: A font file is not just a picture. It can include tiny programs, and a bad one could slow your computer down or hide something sneaky, so be careful which fonts you open.
